children: MARKET WRAPS
STOCKS: Stocks rose after Treasury yields stabilized but gains were muted as oil futures continued climbing due to escalation in the Middle East.
TREASURYS: Treasury yields were mostly lower, though the yield on the 30-year bond was unchanged, hovering near multiyear highs.
FOREX: The U.S. dollar slipped after a weak private-sector jobs survey.
COMMODITIES: Oil futures closed at a six-week high, topping $91 a barrel.
HEADLINES
Google Avoids Breakup of Dominant Ad Tech Business
A federal judge on Wednesday rejected the Justice Department's request
to dismantle Google's online advertising business, the second time a
court has denied government efforts to break up the company after it was
found liable for engaging in illegal monopoly tactics.
The decision is a historical marker that effectively closes the book
on nearly two decades of U.S. antitrust risk for Alphabet's Google,
dating back to when government enforcers during the Obama administration
considered bringing a monopoly case against the company.
It also is another severe blow to an antimonopoly political
movement-at times embraced by both parties-that gained prominence over
the past decade and focused on fighting Silicon Valley. Proponents of
that approach saw antitrust law as the most direct way to break apart
corporate goliaths accused of abusing their power to stifle smaller
competitors.
Uber's $15 Billion Takeover Bid Gets Delivery Hero Board Backing
Delivery Hero confirmed it is in favor of a $14.8 billion takeover bid
from Uber Technologies and advised shareholders to accept it, advancing
the planned tie-up of two of the world's biggest food-delivery platforms.
The German delivery company said Wednesday its management and
supervisory boards had independently reviewed the U.S. giant's offer.
"They deem the offer to be in the best interest of the Company, its
shareholders, employees and other stakeholders," Delivery Hero said.
"They therefore support the offer and recommend that Delivery Hero
shareholders accept it."
Chevron to Invest $7 Billion in Venezuela, Doubling Production
Chevron, Italian oil giant ENI and other energy companies inked deals
Wednesday in Caracas to plow billions of dollars into Venezuela's oil
fields following months of tense negotiations.
The agreements mark the first big win for the Trump administration's
push to revitalize the Latin American country's dilapidated oil industry.
Since ousting strongman Nicolás Maduro in early January, President Trump
has said he intends to secure Western crude supply lines and cut fuel
prices for Americans.
"We were trying to work at what I call Trump speed," Energy Secretary
Chris Wright said at a signing ceremony at the Miraflores Palace.
"President Trump didn't want a nudge or a slow drift in a positive
direction. He wanted to see as fast as possible a transformation in
Venezuela."
Private-Sector Hiring Slowed in August
Hiring by private-sector employers saw softer growth last month,
according to human-resources company ADP.
Private companies added a net 38,000 jobs in August, after adding a
revised 46,000 jobs in July, ADP said. August saw the slowest pace of job
creation since January.
Economists polled by The Wall Street Journal had expected to see
47,000 new private-sector jobs added.
U.S. Government Backs OpenAI in Copyright Fight With Publishers
The U.S. government has filed a statement in support of OpenAI in its
legal battle with the New York Times and other publishers, arguing that
training on news content is within the bounds of "fair use" under U.S.
copyright law.
Making it more difficult for large language models to train on
copyrighted content would be "inconsistent with basic copyright law
principles" and thwart creative and scientific progress, according to a
letter submitted by Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward Jr.
and Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate from the Justice Department.
Fair use is a doctrine that allows for copyright material to be used
without permission in certain circumstances.
Bank of Canada Keeps Rate Steady as Inflation Worries Intensify
OTTAWA-The Bank of Canada left its main interest rate unchanged at
2.25% and adopted a more alarmed tone about the upside risks to inflation
amid new cross-border tariffs and no imminent end to the war in the
Middle East.
Bank of Canada Gov. Tiff Macklem said Wednesday that a sharp
deterioration in U.S.-Canada commercial ties does pose challenges for the
economy, and risks stifling a nascent recovery that suggested businesses
are learning to live with heightened trade-policy uncertainty.
Fresh U.S. tariffs and retaliatory duties from Canada could increase
costs to consumers and pose a drag on growth in the fourth quarter, he
said.
AIG's Zaffino Stepping Down as Chairman, Joining Palantir
American International Group's executive chairman, Peter Zaffino, is
stepping down from the insurer's board and will join data-analytics
company Palantir Technologies as global head of financial services.
AIG on Wednesday said Zaffino will leave the board on Sept. 15, and
that John Rice, a board member since March 2022 who currently serves as
the New York company's lead independent director, will succeed him as
chairman.
Zaffino, who earlier this year retired as AIG's chief executive, will
become a senior adviser, the company said.
Thoma Bravo-Owned Proofpoint in Advanced Talks to Buy Varonis
Thoma Bravo-backed Proofpoint is in advanced talks to buy
cybersecurity firm Varonis Systems, according to people familiar with the
matter.
Varonis had a market value of around $5 billion as of Tuesday
afternoon. Its shares jumped over 10% Wednesday afternoon on news of the
discussions, giving it a market value of around $5.4 billion.
There are no guarantees a deal will come together, as talks could
still fall apart or another suitor could emerge.
TALKING POINT Investor David Booth on Life, Stocks and (Not) Trying to Beat the Market
David Booth launched his investing firm 45 years ago, from his Brooklyn Heights apartment. It just passed $1 trillion in assets under management.

Milestones, and perhaps especially those punctuated with 13-digit achievements, can serve as a good time to reflect, says Booth, the chairman of Dimensional Fund Advisors. And Booth, who turns 80 later this year, is choosing this moment to reflect on his life and five-decade investing career in a new book, "Stay Calm: Learn to Embrace Uncertainty in Investing and Life" (Authors Equity, 220 pgs.).
The book, published Sept. 1, details Booth's early years at the forefront of the index-fund revolution. Investing, he writes, is really just a bet on human innovation-and one that is worth the risks.
In an interview with The Wall Street Journal, Booth discussed why market uncertainty is a good thing, the "miracle" of modern investing access, and why he's optimistic about the future.
WSJ: You spent decades touting passive, follow-the-market stock investing. What's it been like to watch that go from an obscure, unpopular strategy to a dominant force in U.S. investing?

DAVID BOOTH: It's been refreshing. In 1971 when I got out of school, people fought these ideas. You'd talk to fund managers or journalists, and they'd say, "You eggheads. You don't understand markets."

Still, it's not clear how many people have really got the message about how difficult the market is to beat. If you look at the growth in index funds, there's been similar growth in trading volumes. Some people are trading in and out of these, trying to time the market.
Jack Pitcher
